newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- 3-yr Treasury note auction.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- 3-yr Treasury note auction.

text.p: The Treasury's sale of $17.0 billion three-year notes is likely to be the focus of the U.S. government securities market on Tuesday, analysts said.
The three-year sale is the first of a two-part quarterly refunding; the Treasury will sell $12.0 billion in 10-year notes on Wednesday.

The market has rallied for a week, gaining ever since the government reported a much smaller than expected rise in the first-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI). The report made another Federal Reserve rate hike look less inevitable.

William Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Sons, said he thinks the market could be "a little overextended." A a week ago, the 30-year bond yield was just shy of 7.20 percent. On Monday of this week, the bond yield ended at 6.88 percent.
Nevertheless, Hornbarger and other market participants said they did not expect the market to stumble over Tuesday's three-year note auction.
"The pre-auction talk has been pretty good," he said. "People think the market will be able to get the auction done and stay in pretty nice shape."

"It's not that big a deal because three-year issues sort of come and go and I think right now there's nothing to really inhibit market purchases," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Lieberman said that might not have been true a week ago.
"A week ago there was a lot of uncertainty and fear that there might be higher inflation," he said. "Certainly, there was an expectation of higher labor costs. So there was a lot of nervousness.
Lieberman said that now, people's "perspectives are much more relaxed.

William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds, agreed that the market environment has changed a lot from a week ago, boding well for the three-year auction.

"Market psychology has shifted dramatically and against that backdrop, investors, whether domestic or offshore, are willing to accept these spreads," said Sullivan. "Many feel there is genuine value at 6.40 percent or 6.45 percent on the three-year.
In when-issued trade on Monday, the three-year notes to be sold on Tuesday yielded 6.3675 percent.

Lieberman said risk has not disappeared and that many people still think the Fed is likely to tighten monetary policy. But Lieberman said he, himself, is "leaning" against the notion of a Fed tightening at the May 20 policy meeting.

"Things have calmed down quite a bit," said Lieberman. "The Employment Cost Index was very benign. And there's also a budget deal. So it strikes me that it would be a little bit odd for the Fed to tighten policy in the context of relatively good news on inflation, good news on labor costs, and so soon after a budget agreement."

The market will see some new economic data on Tuesday. The BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales index and the Redbook Retail Sales Index are due. "People should be ready for an uptick, at least in the Johnson Redbook," said Elliott Platt, chief economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "Just the way it's calculated will give it an upward bias."

The government will report March factory orders, expected to be down 1.5 percent after a 0.8 percent rise in February, according to economists polled by Reuters. "The orders data we get should replicate the weakness we already saw in the durable goods orders data we got a week ago," said Platt.
